runs.text: ver nem falar, ou não correr com amizade.

lines.note: This continues Soyen from the previous page: people neither see nor speak to one another, or are no longer on friendly terms. The scan reads amizade, not amigade.
Soyenni gozaru gives the expression for being estranged. The Portuguese aßi has the double-s type, rather than the draft’s single ſ.
Com amizade completes the explanation of maintaining friendly relations, here negated by the preceding sentence.
Soyenoqe means adding and taking away. Co- begins cotobano in the illustrative expression about modifying speech.
Cotobano ſoyenoqeuo ſuru concerns additions and omissions in speaking. The Portuguese infinitive is acrecentar, not OCR acrecentat.
The continuation adds diminishing what is said. It completes the two-sided definition of adding and subtracting.
Soyevoqi describes placing something as an addition or attachment. The printed v in the headword and the abbreviated principal forms are retained.
Tando completes ajuntando, followed by por, to put. Together the lines mean putting something down while adding or joining it.
This Sôyǒ denotes large green flies. Both vowel marks are retained independently of the identically spelled entry that follows.

runs.text: Em comũ, ou como os outros.

lines.note: The second Sôyǒ means commonly or like everyone else, with Sônami as its Japanese equivalent. It is separate from the insect name.
Sǒyô denotes leaves of grass or herbs, explained by Cuſano fa. The first caron is faint; the surviving mark, botanical gloss and supplied NINJAL entry support the reading.
Sôyô is explained by Mado and Portuguese Ianelas, windows. The terminal S. is an upright written-register label.
Sǒyô here denotes leaves with frost on them. Ximo and fa supply the components, and the accent pattern is not assimilated to the window entry.
Sǒyocu means both wings. Riǒno tçubaſa confirms the paired or double sense.
Soyogui describes leaves moving or rustling. The principal forms gu and yoida are kept as printed, not expanded to a modern conjugation.

runs.text: aruores, ou eruas com o vento.

lines.note: The movement is caused by wind through trees or herbs. This completes the preceding verb’s explanation.
Sôza is a principal shrine, paraphrased by Tçucaſadoru yaxiro. The Portuguese adjective is divided after princi-.

runs.text: pal dos Camis que he como cabeça das outras.

lines.note: The shrine is described as the head of other kami shrines. Camis occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is recorded for whole-word typeface review.
Sǒza is a seat made of grass, explicitly explained by Cuſano za. It is distinct from the preceding principal-shrine term.

runs.text: Todas as teras, ou ermidas dos mon-

lines.note: Sôzan collectively denotes temples or religious houses. Teras is the Japanese-derived term embedded in the Portuguese description; mon- continues montes below.
Tes completes montes, followed by the countryside. The collective temple term covers religious houses in both settings.

runs.text: Soma, ou cõta em gèral de tudo.

lines.note: Sôzanyô means a total or general reckoning of everything. The printed grave accent in gèral and both circumflexes in the headword are retained.
Sôzô means collectively or in all. The repeated headword begins a question about the total number of people.
Sôzô icutari fodozo asks how many people there are altogether. The Portuguese ends ſão? with a question mark, replacing the garbled OCR ending.
Sǒzocu is transmission or succession, explained by Aitçuzzuqu. The Portuguese definition emphasizes handing something on over time.

runs.text: dalgũa couſa que vem continuada por tempos,

lines.note: What is handed on remains continuous through time. This relative clause expands the preceding transmission or inheritance sense.
The succession can occur through successive holders. Iyeuo sǒzocu ſuru begins the example about the house; the initial s in sǒzocu replaces OCR e.
The Portuguese renders the house example as leaving a house by inheritance. Vo- begins the second example concerning teaching.
Voxiyeuo sǒzocu ſuru concerns handing on a teaching. The Portuguese infinitive is Deixar, not OCR Deixir; tra- begins tradição.

runs.text: dição algũa doutrina pera que ſe và continu-

lines.note: The doctrine is passed down so that it will continue. Both nasal abbreviations and the physical division continu- are retained.
Ando completes continuando, maintaining the transmission of the teaching. The short row is genuine body text.
Sôzocu combines the religious and secular, explicitly paired as Xucqe and zocu. This is distinct from the preceding succession headword.
Secular completes the paired Portuguese description of religious and lay status. It does not begin a new entry.
Sôzôna is qualified by Potiùs, preferring Sôzôxij, with Caximaxij as a Japanese synonym. The Latin editorial word belongs to the italic apparatus.
The adjective describes noise, commotion or disturbance. The gloss explains the shared sense of the preceding Japanese alternatives.
Sozoro describes something done without consideration. The Portuguese adds lack of a definite purpose on the following row.
The action is without purpose or done lightly. Sozo- begins the example sozoro vta rather than another headword.

runs.text: Cantiga que ſe canta aſi ſem propo-

lines.note: Sozoro vta is a song sung casually without a deliberate purpose. The single-s spelling aſi is retained as printed.

runs.text: ſito, & aduertencia como os mininos, ou traba-

lines.note: The casual singing is compared with that of children or workers. Traba- continues trabalhadores on the next line.
Lhadores completes trabalhadores, and fazem closes the comparison with what workers do. This row completes the song example.
Sozorobiqi describes withdrawing an army. The printed principal forms and the closely joined Portuguese oexercito are retained.

runs.text: ou tornar algum tanto pera tras fingidamente.

lines.note: The withdrawal may be a feigned movement somewhat backwards. The scan reads pera, not the OCR paera.
Yumiuo ſozorobiqu means drawing a bow a little. The scan has no extra n after Yumi and no word boundary inside ſozorobiqu.

runs.text: pola corda do arco com a frecha poſta como

lines.note: The bowstring is pulled with the arrow already set in place, as though preparing to shoot. The scan has long ſ in poſta; pola and the historical wording remain unmodernized.
The person acts as though about to shoot. This completes the bow example rather than the earlier military withdrawal.
Sozorodachi means standing somewhere idly, as though waiting. The word eſpe- is physically divided before the next row.

runs.text: rando a alguem ſem fazer nada como ſuſpenſo.

lines.note: The person waits without doing anything, as if suspended or undecided. The abraded word is ſuſpenſo, not two words ſu penſo; the entry continues in column two.
Sozorodachiuo ſuru continues the entry from the first column. Upright X. is the regional label; No begins the contrast with Cami usage.
In the Cami region the expression is Soradachi. Cami belongs within the Portuguese explanation and is a whole-word typeface target.
Sozorogoto denotes something said lightly or without consideration. The qualifying phrase continues on the next row.
The lack of consideration completes the definition. Sozorogotouo begins the verbal example, whose verb follows below.

runs.text: Falar conſigo couſas aßi ſem propoſi-

lines.note: Yǔ completes the example of speaking casually to oneself. The translation’s propoſi- is divided at the physical line end.
To completes propoſito, followed by acting or speaking inconsiderately. This short row finishes the preceding example.
Sozorona and ſozorona coto are alternative adjectival or nominal expressions with the same sense. The lowercase alternative after l is not embedded in Portuguese prose.
Sozoroni is the adverb meaning lightly or without order. Adu. belongs to the italic grammatical apparatus.
Sôzôxij describes noisy commotion or disturbance. Its two circumflexes agree with the related adjective earlier on the page.
Sôzôxiſa and Sôzôxǔ give the related noun and adverbial form. They remain on their shared physical line and are not separate Portuguese glosses.
Sôzzucaſa denotes the head or chief of everyone collectively. The long s in caſa is retained independently of the supplied index’s normalized spelling.
SV means a bird’s nest. The initial S is enlarged across this line and the next; it is not OCR C, and Suuo caqu- begins the nest-building example.
Ru completes caquru, with cǔ offered as an alternative form, both glossed as making a nest. The apparent OCR P was the lower part of the preceding enlarged S, not additional text.
Fa- from the previous line joins naruru to form fanaruru. Suuo fanaruru and ſudachiuo ſuru mean leaving the nest; the line ends with a period, not a hyphen.
Suuo tatçu and ſubanareuo ſuru are additional expressions with the same nest-leaving sense. Idem closes this entry.

runs.text: Coroa de area, reſtinga, ou baixo darea fo-

lines.note: This Su denotes a sandbank, shoal or sandy spit. The definition specifies soft sand, with fo- continuing fofa below.

runs.text: fa, onde ſe acaruão os pès deſembarcandoſe,

lines.note: The description relates the soft sand to people’s feet when disembarking. The printed acaruão is retained; its precise historical verb identification remains uncertain, without altering the clear sandbank sense.
Suſaqi is referred to its own alphabetical entry. The Latin direction is Vide ſuo loco, with long s, not OCR fuo.
Another Su means vinegar. Su aye introduces food prepared with vinegar, whose explanation continues below.
The food explanation ends with vinagre. Suuo cǒ then introduces an idiomatic expression for inciting or provoking someone, not a recipe instruction.

runs.text: uocar a alguem a que peleje, &c.

lines.note: The provocation is to make someone fight. This completes the figurative example attached to the vinegar entry.

runs.text: Eſteira rala de caninhas, ou outra couſa,

lines.note: This Su is a loosely woven mat of small canes or comparable material. Its architectural use is explained on the following lines.

runs.text: que poem de baixo da palha do telhado quando

lines.note: The mat is placed beneath roof thatch. The dictionary preserves the separate words de baixo.
The mat is used when roofing houses. Suuo amu gives the expression for weaving it, followed by the Portuguese verb Fazer.
Eſtas eſteiras completes the translation as making these mats. It remains a separate continuation row.

runs.text: Hũa figura, ou pintura dos veſtidos, à

lines.note: Suama denotes a textile design or painted garment pattern. The shape of the pattern is compared with waterways below.

runs.text: maneiradas voltas, & entradas q̃ tẽ os rios, ou

lines.note: The pattern resembles bends and inlets in rivers or shorelines. The close printed maneiradas is retained; the abbreviated words q̃ tẽ are separated as visible.
Prayas adds beaches or shores to the comparison. This single-word continuation completes the design description.
Suaxi, equated with Fadaxi, means barefoot. Suaxi- begins the illustrative phrase on the next line.
Suaxide ayumu means going or walking barefoot. The Portuguese reads Ir and the single word descalço, correcting OCR Is and des calço.
Subacu is followed by Meliùs, preferring Sunbacu. The historical definition describes an abdominal illness or pain; it is transcribed, not adopted as a modern diagnosis.

runs.text: de barriga cauſada de hum bicho comprido,

lines.note: The historical explanation attributes the abdominal pain to a long worm. The description continues with its width and supposed movement.

runs.text: & largo, o qual pretende ir ter à bolſa dos

lines.note: The worm is described as broad and as tending toward a bodily pouch. These are the dictionary’s historical explanatory claims.
The destination is specified as the scrotum or the legs. The line completes the historical illness account without replacing it with modern medical terminology.
Subari means becoming narrow or constricted. Item introduces a further use relating to pronunciation.

runs.text: nunciarſe com certo acento lene como dizer

lines.note: The pronunciation sense involves a certain gentle or close accent. The dictionary illustrates its terminology with Portuguese and Japanese words on the next row.
Auô is the Portuguese example and Qeô the Japanese one. The whole Portuguese word is italic; Qeô is upright and its circumflex is preserved, not redistributed among letters.
Cuchiga ſubaru means the mouth becomes small or pursed. The opening paragraph mark is present in the scan, and peque- begins pequena.
The narrowing is accomplished by drawing in the lips. Fitono xin- starts a new example about a person’s means or estate.
Fitono xindaiga xidaini ſubatte yuqu describes someone’s resources gradually contracting. Ho- begins the Portuguese homem on the next line.
The person grows poorer and declines in estate or condition. This completes the figurative use of contraction.
Subaru is glossed Sete eſtrello. The printed singular-looking form is retained rather than silently replacing it with the modern plural estrelas.
Subaruboxi has the same referent as Subaru. Idem explicitly links the two names.
Sube means a way, means or manner. Mono yǔ begins the example about speaking, and no terminal period is visible after yǔ.

runs.text: Não ſabe o modo como ha

lines.note: Mono yǔ ſubeuo xiranu means not knowing how to speak. The Portuguese has ha, completing ha de falar on the next row, rather than OCR ba.
De falar completes the speaking example. The separate right-hand Sube is the catchword for the following page and is now recorded in its own furniture zone.
